Find the particular solution to the differential equation y′=sin⁡(3x)cos⁡(2y) that satisfies y(0)=0. Assume that −π4<y<π4.

a
3sin⁡(2y)=2(1−cos⁡(3x))
b
sin⁡(2y)=1−cos⁡(3x)
c
sin⁡(2y)=cos⁡(3x)
d

e

decision.explanation: Separate variables: cos(2y) dy = sin(3x) dx. Integrating gives (1/2)sin(2y) = -(1/3)cos(3x) + C. Since y(0)=0, C=1/3, so 3sin(2y)=2(1-cos(3x)), which is option a.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}$ that satisfies $y(0)=0.$ Assume that $-\frac{\pi }{4}<y<\frac{\pi }{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)} \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ \int (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${C}_{1}=2C.$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find ${C}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the above equation as

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)).
$$

content.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}$ that satisfies $y(0)=0.$ Assume that $-\frac{\pi }{4}<y<\frac{\pi }{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)} \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ \int (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${C}_{1}=2C.$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find ${C}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the above equation as

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)).
$$

decision.explanation: Separating variables gives e^y dy=e^(4x) dx, so e^y=e^(4x)/4+C. Applying y(0)=5 yields C=e^5-1/4. Thus y=ln((e^(4x)+4e^5-1)/4), which is option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x-y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=5.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=5$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4\cdot 0}}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \frac{1}{4}+C & ={e}^{5} \\ C & =\frac{4{e}^{5}-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=5$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}+4{e}^{5}-1}{4}).
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
content.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x-y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=5.$
content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=5$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4\cdot 0}}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \frac{1}{4}+C & ={e}^{5} \\ C & =\frac{4{e}^{5}-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=5$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4x}+4{e}^{5}-1}{4}).
$$

after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-4\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{4}-{2}^{3}-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{8-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ is

$$

content.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}.$
content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-4\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{4}-{2}^{3}-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{8-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$
